newsitem.title: USA: U.N. chief calls on U.S. to invest in diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief calls on U.S. to invest in diplomacy.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan ended his visit to the U.S. capital on Friday with praise and promises from congressional critics to work toward solving the U.N. financial crisis caused by the United States.

The good news for Annan, on his first official trip since he began his five-year term on Jan. 1, was the number of officials who lined up to see him and lauded his commitment to reforming and restructuring the world body.

But the bad news was the many conditions that emerged in talks with Republican congressmen on how much money the United States would pay of its $1.3 billion debt, when anything would be paid and what its U.N. dues would be in the future.

For his part, Annan said he was determined to use the authority of the secretary-general to push reform. "Not reform for its own sake but in order to revitalise the organisation's capacity to serve its members in our changing world."

In an address to the National Press Club, he repeated a similar message he gave to Congress: "War is the failure of diplomacy, then surely diplomacy is our first line of defence." He said the world spent billions preparing for war, so "shouldn't we spend a billion or two preparing for peace?
"Where we have differences, let us address them openly and honestly. But let us at last put an end to the accusations, counter-accusations and name-calling," he said.
Annan began his trip on Monday in an effort to institute a "time of healing" with the United States and collect the arrears for regular dues and peacekeeping Washington owes.
A 59-year-old, soft-spoken Ghanaian, he was elected last month after the Clinton administration forced Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt out of office for allegedly not moving fast enough on reform.
Newt Gingrich, speaker of the House of Representatives, said Annan showed a "refreshingly new attitude" toward working with the United States. "I think we will be able to work this out," he said.
And Representative Robert Livingston, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, said he looked forward to eliminating the U.S. debt in "some sort of workable fashion."
But he said he wanted the United Nations to explain why it puts the U.S. debt at $1.3 billion, when according to his calculations it is $825 million.

U.N. officials say the discrepancy lies in unilateral decisions by Congress over the years to eliminate certain programmes or lower U.S. contributions unilaterally. In 1994 Congress eliminated the surchage of five percent levied on key Security Council members for peacekeeping missions. This lowered the U.S. assessment to 25 percent.

Many congressmen now are insisting that Washington pay only 20 percent, rather than 25 percent of the regular U.N. budget. Annan said assessments were made on the basis of the U.S. share of the world economy, currently 27 percent.
He said he personally did not object to lower dues for the United States, but that these issues had to be decided by the 185 U.N. members.
Sen. Ted Stevens of Alaska, the head of the Senate Appropriations Committee, said the United States should get credit from the world body for voluntary contributions.

"I don't think we (Congress) will be willing to pay an advance without real compliance with a new set of reforms with regard to how American dollars are spent and what credits we get for what we do in kind for the U.N.," he said.
Questioned about this, Annan said individual nations could not decide which special assignments to undertake and "then pass the bill on to the United Nations."

Annan on Thursday also met at length with Sen. Jesse Helms and his Senate Foreign Relations Committee and agreed that regular consultations were needed between the committee staff and U.N. officials. Helms, a North Carolina Republican who has in effect demanded the United Nations be shut down, said he was drafting legislation with "benchmarks for U.N. reform."
Asked about Helms, Annan denied the senator was imposing conditions or that he was accepting any. "I came here to say what we are going to do ... to clear up misunderstanding."
But he quipped later that other states that owed money to the United Nations had not "imposed any benchmarks."
